comments.author: theptip
comments.text:
I think there is a massive opportunity for this kind of feed disaggregation. Used to be the recommender and indexing of content was hard, now I believe we can likely build our own according to our own preferences.
Haiku/Sonnet (or even Jev) can do a lot of the filtering work to rank and extend an RSS feed list.
I think this gives us an opportunity to fully cut the cord from eyeball merchants who want us to maximally engage and therefore polarize their content.
The big remaining hook will be the social graph; I am interested to see how far the EU push for mandatory interoperability will go. Another angle I’d support would be mandatory pluggable standards for your own ranking algorithm, but it captures less of the win than full disaggregation.

I am not aware of any economically feasible way to run my 5+ ton HVAC system full-time on batteries after a hurricane just reset all the infrastructure, and you do need to run it full time because of the insane humidity and latent heat that follows a tropical system. Doing the math, I'd need something approaching 800kWh of storage to ride through this kind of event (7+ days). This is approaching half a million dollars in batteries. I can install an
extremely

I think a simple generator on an ATS remains undefeated from an engineering perspective. If you have an air cooled unit, the maintenance is not much more complicated than with a lawnmower. comments.author: amluto
comments.text:
A fundamental problem here is that V2H during an outage requires a disconnection device (in the NEC this is a “microgrid interconnect device”), and the manufacturers of such things have made no effort whatsoever to standardize the control protocol.  This means that you cannot build an islanded-V2H-ready house and just plug in a car.  So the whole concept is kind of dead in the water.
At least Tesla is vertically integrated enough to pull it off within their own product portfolio, but this has approximately no value if you want to use a non-Tesla car.

comments.author: 1dom
comments.text:
This entire area is a mess, I spent a year or so trying to get bidirectional charging set up at home in the UK. I even went to several of the vendors mentioned in that post and said "I've got basically a blank cheque and permission to do whatever you want however you want, even use it all as a case study to make this work" and nowhere could/would do it.
The most frustrating thing is it looks like V2G is easier and more accessible than V2H[1]: it's easier to give control of your battery to your energy provider and bypass your house to help the energy companies than it is just to power your own home with your own car battery.
Technically, this is ridiculous. You don't bypass your house when you do V2G.

stories.title_en: One-minute frequency disturbances from synchronization in power systems

comments.author: schiffern
comments.text:
The corresponding concept in gears is to avoid meshing two gears unless the number of teeth are co-prime, because this will cause uneven wear patterns. If the tooth counts are coprime, then each tooth will contact every tooth on the other gear the same number of times, effectively "wear leveling" the teeth.
In this instance, one fix is to fire the timer every 59.XXX seconds, so it will naturally drift out of phase with the minute hand of the clock.
If work needs to be done exactly every 60 seconds, this is fixed by having a WAIT(RAND(60e6)) microseconds during the first timer initialization, so if 10,000 units start simultaneously they don't try all at once. This is good practice in most (all?) systems. Hint: test power and infra outage/reconnect, which can unintentionally sync timers.
This is why many software will do automated updates every 17 hours: 17 is coprime with 24.
Classic "thundering herd" mitigation tactics.
Edit: Tempting to blame IoT, but (since this is news) I don't think anyone knew there was something to fix here. We have the tools however.

comments.author: kazinator
comments.text:
I'm skeptical that this one minute jitter period is solely attributable to one minute timers in power inverter equipment. It's likely the net scale effect of all cron-like scheduling of actions in everything with a microprocessor. All the long-term scheduling that is done with minute precision (i.e. seconds field is implicitly :00) regardless of its individual period.  Like if one device is scheduling at x:17 and x:47 every hour, another one is doing x:06, x:09, x:12, x:15, ... and numerous other combinations, at scale, the common divisor will be one minute. If wall clock time is used, all the devices that are synchronized to a network time will have cron-like scheduling events firing at xx:xx:00 for all values of x.
This type of scheduling should be randomized at the seconds level, perhaps. Unfortunately, it would require a massively coordinated effort across numerous operating system and application stacks.

Here's the NIST link:
https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-98432
Here are my notes so far after digging into this with Claude + defensive access:
1. Not just an MPTCP thing - any received IPv4 packet with options creates the problematic conditions.
2. Also appears that using NetLabel/CIPSO (SELinux or Smack with a CIPSOV4 mapping) creates the same conditions that a packet with IP options would. If you're using these, it might mean that dropping IPv4 packets with IP options might not fully mitigate.

.
Fastmail does support MTA-STS for inbound messages... sort of. For inbound MTA-STS the email provider needs to use a TLS certificate issued by a trusted certificate authority, which Fastmail does. Additionally, the domain name in the "to address" needs to enable MTA-STS using some DNS records. Fastmail does not provide the documentation for setting this up, although they have decent adoption by folks who figured it out on their own. I'm seeing about 0.2% of domains using Fastmail enforce MTA-STS inbound:
SELECT mta_sts_mode, COUNT(*) AS "count"
FROM read_parquet('dns-analytics-2026-q3-*.parquet')
WHERE exchange_suffix = 'messagingengine.com'
GROUP BY mta_sts_mode
ORDER BY count DESC;
---
mta_sts_mode  count
-             174,877
enforce       354
testing       313
none          11
This is about the same as Protonmail (~0.2%)

Not sure why so many things use the compatibility form of normalisation.
Some older RFCs even recommended using it for passwords, which needlessly reduces entropy (yes we need to normalise passwords because of combining characters, but we don’t need to collapse symbols that a user can choose from, like ſ and s).
In my opinion, the compatibility form makes mostly sense for searching text, and even then it’s sometimes annoying (I want to search exactly for ss and not ß, browser). If you know of other good use cases let me know.
It also OK to disallow registering two identifiers with the same compatibility normalisation form (edit: this does not prevent all homoglyph attacks BTW, that is another can of worms), but I don’t see the need to normalise the identifier when it’s used.
